messages.subject: Missing data from sampling,
parts:
> >
> > Len, and others,
> >

Thank you for your good discussion on point and transect sampling but my
concern is with a private contractor who has a sampling plan and then is not
able to follow it completely because a sampling staff member is sick or a
car breaks down or the weather is too rotten to see anything. These all in
zero observations for that particular time but the zeros are misleading. In
cancer research, Rubin and Gary King and others have developed some fairly
robust imputation methods that should help give more reliable and valid
results than if we reduce the sampling events or use zero.

I was hoping someone had used a jackknife technique or something similar to
give us an idea of how much we can impute missing values of different types
without falling off a high cliff.

Second, and not totally unrelated, is anyone looking at mimicry using
Distance-Sampling?

Dwight Hines
IndyMedia
Maine, USA

> >
> > I guess you're referring to Lisa Baril's message of 12/Sept and Steve's
> > reply of 13/Sept.
> >
> > If Lisa wants to estimate density by year and point, then she says that
> > some points were not surveyed in the first year, and so clearly this
> > will not be possible. But this is not a problem for the subsequent
> > model she will be building so long as the probability of missing a point
> > is not correlated with the density being especially low or high, given
> > the habitat etc. (in other words, so long as the reason for the data
> > being missing is "ignorable").
> >
> > (The modelling approach is outlined in the paper Steve Buckland referred
> > to -- I didn't see the explicit reference in his posting so here it is:
> > Buckland, S.T., Russell, R.E., Dickson, B.G., Saab, V.A., Gorman, D.G.
> > and Block, W.M. 2009. Analysing designed experiments in distance
> > sampling. Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Environmental
> > Statistics 14, 432-442.
> > and it's available here:
> > http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/buckland%20et%20al%20jabes%202009.pdf
> > )
> >
> > If she just wants to estimate density by point, pooled across years,
> > then there are no points without any surveys, so it's no problem at all
> > (again, so long as the variation between number of visits is not related
> > to density). The effort per point is the total number of visits.
> >
> > I emphasize that the modelling approach is not currently available in
> > Distance -- such analyses need to be programmed in a stats package such
> > as R, which might call the distance analysis engine to calculate
> > detection probabilities or related quantities. If you are stuck on how
> > to do this, it might be helpful to look at a report by Eric Rexstad that
> > gives an example of doing distance sampling analyses in R, at
> > http://hdl.handle.net/10023/629
> > or contact Prof. Buckland for a copy of his code. One day these things
> > will be available in the Distance interface, I hope!

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Missing data from sampling,
parts:
On 16/09/2010 09:44, Dwight Hines wrote:
>> >> Len, and others,
>> >>
> > Thank you for your good discussion on point and transect sampling but my
> > concern is with a private contractor who has a sampling plan and then is not
> > able to follow it completely because a sampling staff member is sick or a
> > car breaks down or the weather is too rotten to see anything. These all in
> > zero observations for that particular time but the zeros are misleading. In
> > cancer research, Rubin and Gary King and others have developed some fairly
> > robust imputation methods that should help give more reliable and valid
> > results than if we reduce the sampling events or use zero.
> >
> > I was hoping someone had used a jackknife technique or something similar to
> > give us an idea of how much we can impute missing values of different types
> > without falling off a high cliff.
This seems to reflect a misunderstanding of what distance sampling
does. If there is no effort, there is no zero in the data. Generally,
if a line or point could not be surveyed when intended, it would be
surveyed later. If this is not feasible, as can occur with shipboard
surveys for example, there is a gap in the effort. That can cause
problems if for example missing effort is correlated with animal
density. If that is thought to occur, the DSM engine of Distance can be
used to fit a spatial model for density, which does 'impute missing
values' in the sense that it gives you estimates of animal density at
locations without effort.

> > Second, and not totally unrelated, is anyone looking at mimicry using
> > Distance-Sampling?
Less cryptic comments might elicit a response!

Steve Buckland
